newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Moroccan king urges Israel to return to Peres's way.
newsitem.headline: Moroccan king urges Israel to return to Peres's way.

text.p: Moroccan King Hassan, in an interview published on Tuesday, said the Middle East peace process was in crisis and Israel needed to return to the path taken by its previous government.
He told visiting regional French journalists: "We are in a state of crisis. We must not hide this. It is a crisis which, unfortunately, screens the horizon over 180 degrees of the visual field."

In the interview, carried by the official Moroccan news agency MAP, the king recalled that after defeat in the 1967 Middle East war, the Arabs had rejected three proposals - recognition of Israel, negotiations, and peace with the Jewish state.
"Thirty years after, it is the Israeli government which...in its turn expresses three other "No-es" -- no land for peace, no Palestinian state, no discussions on Jerusalem."
Israel has taken a hard line on negotiations since Benjamin Netanyahu defeated former prime minister Shimon Peres in May elections.

Earlier this month, Netanyahu said: "You can dream every night...and you will still wake up every morning and see: There is no Palestinian state...there is not and there will not be a Palestinian state."

Netanyahu has also rejected the principle of swapping land for peace -- effectively a pullout from the Golan Heights captured from Syria in 1967, and from Israel's occupation zone in southern Lebanon.
King Hassan said he believed the peace process was "irreversible and what I would like to see is that the Israeli government understands. It is irreversible."
The king, one of the architects of secret peace moves that led to the Madrid 1991 peace conference, said: "In any case, according to its acts, it (Israel) does not appear to have understood."

He said he had made no proposals to get the peace process back on track, adding: "The best proposition I have is that we return to matters in the way they were left by the preceding (Israeli) government...The Israeli state, if it wants to be credible, must respect this continuity of the state."
